reading.h2: The Ancient Faith: Early Church Fathers and the Path of the Tewahedo Church

reading.p: This lesson traces the apostolic roots of the Church, the great Christological conflict of the fifth century, and how the Ethiopian Tewahedo Church received and preserved the Miaphysite faith through her Fathers, councils, and monasteries.

The earliest Church was an organic network of local communities. Authority gradually consolidated around Apostolic Sees — cities where the Apostles or their immediate disciples founded major, influential churches. By the fourth century (at the Council of Nicaea, 325 AD), three Sees held primary jurisdiction across broad regions: Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch. These were the indisputable ancient powerhouses.

The Pentarchy (rule of five) was a later imperial plan to formalize the five supreme Sees, strategically adding Constantinople and Jerusalem. The system was based on the belief that these Patriarchs, acting collectively, safeguarded the universal faith — with authority residing in the Ecumenical Councils, not in the singular power of any one See.

list: Rome — St. Peter and St. Paul
Alexandria — St. Mark the Evangelist
Antioch — St. Peter
Constantinople — St. Andrew the Apostle
Jerusalem — St. James the Just

reading.h2: 1,600 Years of Unity: Alexandria and the Ethiopian Episcopal Line

reading.p: The Patriarchate of Alexandria (the Coptic Church) was one of the three original and most influential Apostolic Sees, along with Rome and Antioch. It was traditionally founded by St. Mark the Evangelist, the author of the Gospel of Mark. Alexandria became the intellectual and theological capital of early Christianity, wielding immense authority over all of Africa and establishing the standards for biblical scholarship and doctrine.

This link began when St. Frumentius (Abune Selama) was consecrated as the first Bishop of Aksum by St. Athanasius, Pope of Alexandria, around 330 AD. The Church in the Aksumite Kingdom (modern Ethiopia and Eritrea) was directly under Alexandria’s spiritual jurisdiction for over 1,600 years.

reading.h2: The Accepted Councils (Nicaea I, Constantinople I, Ephesus I)

reading.p: Three great councils form the undisputed foundation of the Tewahedo faith.

list: Nicaea I (325 AD): against Arianism (which claimed Christ was a created being). Affirmation: Christ is fully God — Jesus is of the same divine nature as God the Father.

Constantinople I (381 AD): against Macedonianism (which denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit). Affirmation: the Holy Spirit is fully God — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three distinct Persons who are equally divine.

Ephesus I (431 AD): against Nestorianism (which divided Christ into two separate persons). Affirmation: Christ is one Person — God and Man are perfectly and inseparably united in Jesus Christ. Mary is called Theotokos (God-bearer) because she gave birth to the one Person who is God.

reading.p: All major ancient Christian Churches — Oriental Orthodox, Eastern Orthodox, and Roman Catholic — share and uphold the definitions set forth by the first three Ecumenical Councils. The Tewahedo Church uses these councils as the undisputed foundation for its doctrine on the Trinity and the Incarnation.

After the first three councils affirmed that Christ is fully God and fully Man, and one Person, a crucial question remained: How exactly are His divine nature and human nature united in that one Person? This debate was known as the Christological Controversy. Disagreeing on the precise wording to describe this union led directly to the first major split in the ancient Church.

reading.h2: The Christological Dilemma — Two Main Camps

reading.p: By the mid-fifth century, two main schools of thought dominated the debate.

This school emphasized the complete unity of the natures after the Incarnation, fearing any language that seemed to separate Christ’s divinity and humanity. Its doctrine argued that the natures are made “one” and work together as a single Divine-Human entity (Miaphysitism, or Tewahedo). Its key figure was St. Cyril of Alexandria, whose formula was central to the Council of Ephesus.

This school emphasized the need to clearly affirm that Christ’s divinity and humanity remained distinct after the Incarnation, fearing language that suggested the Divine swallowed up or confused the human nature. Its doctrine maintained that Christ exists “in two natures” (Dyophysitism). Its key figure was Pope Leo I of Rome, whose Tome was central to the Council of Chalcedon.

Convened by the Roman Emperor Marcian in 451 AD, this council was called to definitively resolve the Christological conflict between Alexandria and Antioch. It affirmed the doctrine that Christ is “one and the same Son… acknowledged in two natures” (in duabus naturis). This core statement is known as Dyophysitism, the Greek term for “two natures.”

The Chalcedonian Definition sought to be a balanced compromise by defining how the two natures exist within Christ, using four negative adverbs to guard against heresy. The natures were said to be united:

list: Without Confusion (Asynchytos): to guard against the Alexandrian extreme, which the Dyophysites called “Eutychianism.”
Without Change (Atreptos): to guard against the idea that the Divine Nature was altered.
Without Division (Adiairetos): to guard against the Antiochian extreme (Nestorianism).
Without Separation (Achoristos): to guard against the final separation of the Person.

reading.p: The Alexandrian (Coptic) delegation, led by Pope Dioscorus, absolutely rejected the Chalcedonian phrase “in two natures” (en duo physeis). Their theological fear was that this wording risked a return to the heresy of Nestorianism, which divided Christ into two separate persons or subjects.

Alexandria insisted instead on the formula of St. Cyril — “One Incarnate Nature of God the Word” — believing that after the Incarnation the two natures became one unified reality (Tewahedo / Miaphysite). The council deposed and exiled Pope Dioscorus, effectively marking the permanent administrative and theological schism.

The Churches that rejected the Council of Chalcedon became known historically as the Non-Chalcedonian Churches, or the Oriental Orthodox family. This marks the moment the ancient Apostolic Sees of Alexandria (Coptic), Antioch (Syriac), and Aksum (Tewahedo) officially separated from the Patriarchates of Rome, Constantinople, and Jerusalem.

The theological position of the Tewahedo Church and the entire Oriental Orthodox family is Miaphysitism (Greek for “one nature”). This doctrine affirms that, after the Incarnation, Christ possesses one incarnate nature of God the Word, united from the divine and the human. The two natures are perfectly and perpetually joined — without confusion, change, division, or separation — so that Christ is one, while each nature keeps its own properties.

Miaphysitism is based on the formula of St. Cyril of Alexandria: “One Incarnate Nature of God the Word.” To visualize this union, the Tewahedo Fathers used the analogy of fire and iron: the fire and iron become one glowing, inseparable piece, but the iron does not cease to be iron, and the fire does not cease to be fire.

The term Tewahedo is the Ge’ez word — Ge’ez being the ancient liturgical language of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Churches — that translates directly to “made one” or “unity.” It is the native theological equivalent of the Greek Miaphysitism. The term is so central to the Church’s identity that it is part of its official name: the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

Tewahedo expresses the core belief that the Divine Nature and the Human Nature of Jesus Christ are permanently and perfectly united in the one Person of God the Word — the one incarnate nature of the Word, united from two. This unity is without separation, without confusion, and without change: both natures, with their full properties, are preserved (as the iron does not cease to be iron, nor the fire to be fire), while remaining inseparably one in Christ. It is not a mixing or absorption of the humanity into the divinity, which the Church rejects as the error of Eutyches.

In the late fifth and early sixth centuries, right after the theological turmoil of the Council of Chalcedon, a revered group of missionaries — traditionally numbering Nine Saints — arrived in the Aksumite Kingdom. Many were believed to be Byzantine monks or clerics who fled the Roman Empire because of their rejection of the Chalcedonian Dyophysite doctrine. They sought refuge and a fertile ground for their Miaphysite faith.

Their arrival was critical in solidly establishing the Alexandrian theological position in the Ethiopian Highlands; they were missionaries of the Tewahedo faith. They introduced and formalized the structures of intensive monasticism, creating spiritual centers that became essential for preserving the faith during later centuries of isolation. They were also instrumental in finalizing and standardizing the translation of the Bible and key liturgical texts into the classical Ethiopian language, Ge’ez.

reading.h2: Monasteries and the Nine Founding Fathers

reading.p: Each saint is associated with establishing a key monastery that served as a center for theology, education, and cultural preservation, primarily located in the regions of Tigray (Ethiopia) and Eritrea. These monasteries became the strongholds of the Miaphysite faith.

list: Debre Damo: founded by Abba Aragawi, this is one of Ethiopia’s oldest monasteries, famously located on a flat-topped mountain accessible only by a rope.

Abba Garima Monastery: founded by Abba Garima, this monastery is the custodian of the Garima Gospels, some of the oldest illuminated Christian manuscripts in the world, dated to the 5th–7th centuries.
Debre Zewayt / Qorqor: associated with figures like Abba Aftse.

reading.p: The Tewahedo tradition venerates these specific figures as the fathers of Ethiopian monasticism. They are traditionally named:

list: Abba Aftse
Abba Alef
Abba Aragawi (or Za-Mika’el)
Abba Garima
Abba Guba
Abba Liqanos
Abba Pantelewon
Abba Sehma
Abba Yem’ata

reading.p: Several Fathers laid and preserved the foundation of the Tewahedo faith.

list: St. Ignatius of Antioch (c. 35 – c. 108 AD): author of seven epistles and an early defender of the reality of Christ’s flesh; his fierce defense of the undivided unity of Christ’s person laid the groundwork for Miaphysite theology.

St. Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296 – 373 AD): author of On the Incarnation of the Word, who consecrated the first Bishop of Aksum (St. Frumentius), establishing the Alexandrian authority over the Tewahedo Church.
St. Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376 – 444 AD): author of the Twelve Anathemas against Nestorius, whose formula, ‘One Incarnate Nature of God the Word,’ is the canonical basis for the Tewahedo doctrine.

Pope Dioscorus I of Alexandria (d. 454 AD): the primary figure who rejected the Chalcedonian Creed and was deposed, causing the official schism between the Oriental Orthodox and the rest of the Church.
The Nine Saints (late 5th century): founders of monastic orders who solidified the Miaphysite position in the Ethiopian Highlands and finalized the translation of the Ge’ez Bible.

studyGuide.overview: This lesson follows the path of the ancient faith from the apostolic Sees and the Pentarchy through the first three Ecumenical Councils to the great fifth-century Christological controversy. It explains why the Tewahedo Church, following St. Cyril’s Miaphysite formula, rejected the Council of Chalcedon, and how St. Frumentius, the Nine Saints, and the Fathers established and preserved the Tewahedo faith in Ethiopia.
keyPoints: The three original Apostolic Sees were Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch; the Pentarchy later added Constantinople and Jerusalem, with authority residing in the Ecumenical Councils.
Ethiopia’s episcopal line began with St. Frumentius, consecrated by St. Athanasius of Alexandria around 330 AD, linking Aksum to Alexandria for over 1,600 years.
The Tewahedo Church accepts the first three councils: Nicaea (against Arianism), Constantinople (against Macedonianism), and Ephesus (against Nestorianism, affirming the Theotokos).
The Christological controversy concerned how Christ’s two natures are united in one Person.
The Tewahedo Church holds Miaphysitism — St. Cyril’s ‘One Incarnate Nature of God the Word’ — and rejects Chalcedon’s ‘in two natures.’
‘Tewahedo’ is Ge’ez for ‘made one,’ expressing union without separation, confusion, or change, with the natures’ properties preserved.
The Nine Saints brought the Miaphysite faith, established monasteries, and helped finalize the Ge’ez Bible.
reviewQuestions: What were the three original Apostolic Sees, and how did the Pentarchy come about?
How did the Ethiopian Church become linked to Alexandria, and through whom?
Which three councils does the Tewahedo Church accept, and what heresy did each address?
What was the central question of the Christological controversy?
Why did Pope Dioscorus and the Alexandrian delegation reject the phrase ‘in two natures’?
What does ‘Tewahedo’ mean, and how does the fire-and-iron analogy explain it?
Who were the Nine Saints, and what was their contribution to the Tewahedo Church?

checks: First three Ecumenical Councils (Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus) affirmed as foundational
Council of Chalcedon and its ‘in two natures’ formula correctly NOT accepted
Miaphysite union affirmed and correctly distinguished from confusion/absorption; fire-and-iron analogy keeps natures’ properties intact (not monophysitism)
Nestorianism explicitly rejected; Theotokos affirmed via Ephesus
St. Cyril’s ‘One Incarnate Nature of God the Word’ presented as the canonical basis
Ge’ez term Tewahedo correctly defined as ‘made one’ — union without separation, confusion, or change
Historical account of Pope Dioscorus, the Nine Saints, and the Alexandria–Aksum link consistent with Tewahedo tradition
